symptoms: Rapidly expanding water-soaked dark olive to purplish-black lesions on leaf tips or margins
Delicate white cottony/downy fungal-like growth visible on leaf undersides during moist early mornings
Stems develop dark brown to black greasy-looking necrotic lesions
Entire canopy collapses with a characteristic pungent rot smell in severe outbreaks
management: Treat suspected late blight as an emergency; pathogen can destroy an entire field within 7-10 days in wet highland conditions.
Rogue and safely bag isolated severely infected plants without shaking spores onto neighbors.
Contact your nearest Sub-County Agricultural Officer or KALRO station immediately for current registered blight controls and preventative spray intervals.
Hilling up (earthing up) tubers well with soil prevents wash-down of sporangia onto developing tubers.
prevention: Plant certified clean potato seed and consider late blight tolerant varieties bred by KALRO/CIP (e.g., Shangi, Unica, Asante where available).
Completely destroy discard piles (culls) from previous harvest—they are the primary inoculum reservoir in Kenya.
Maximize plant spacing and orientation toward prevailing winds to promote fast canopy drying.
monitoring: Scout the field daily during cool, foggy, overcast, or rainy weather (temperatures 10-20°C, RH > 90%).
Inspect lower leaves, leaf undersides, and depressed wet spots in the field first thing in the morning.
escalation: White sporulation observed on leaf undersides.
More than 5% of plants exhibiting water-soaked black lesions in cool rainy periods.
Stem lesions detected on multiple plants across the plot.
kenya_notes: The single most devastating disease of potato in Kenya highlands (Nyandarua, Mau Narok, Meru, Elgeyo Marakwet). In wet seasons, farmers without timely intervention often suffer 80-100% loss.
